terms.comment: Horace’s words to Trebatius. Nequeō is the plain “I can’t” of comedy and conversation; nōn possum dormīre says the same.

terms.gloss: be unable to get to sleep
evidence: Cic. Tusc. 4.44: quod somnum capere nōn posset

phrases.latin: Pater, dormīre nequeō. — Assidēbō tibi, dum obdormīscis.
phrases.english: Dad, I can’t sleep. — I’ll sit with you until you drop off.

phrases.latin: Noctū experrēctus sum nec rūrsus obdormīscere potuī.
phrases.english: I woke up in the night and couldn’t get back to sleep.

phrases.latin: peream male, sī nōn optimum erat; vērum nequeō dormīre
phrases.english: hang me if that wouldn’t be best; but I can’t sleep

phrases.latin: noctū ambulābat in pūblicō Themistoclēs, quod somnum capere nōn posset
phrases.english: Themistocles used to walk about the streets at night, because he could not get to sleep

phrases.latin: nē eās quidem continuās, sed ut in illō temporis spatiō ter aut quater expergīscerētur
phrases.english: not even those hours unbroken, but so that in that time he woke three or four times

sources: Lewis & Short: nequeo · Lewis & Short: insomnia · Lewis & Short: obdormisco
